title: The Birth of the Monkey King
content_zh:
In the Eastern Continent, on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, a great boulder sat upon the peak. Since the creation of the world, this rock had absorbed the pure essence of Heaven and the subtle virtues of Earth, the nourishment of the sun and the baptism of the moon. One day, it cracked open with a thunderous roar, and from within burst forth a stone egg.
The stone egg was carried by the wind until it transformed into a stone monkey, complete with all five senses and four limbs. The monkey opened his eyes, and two beams of golden light shot straight through the celestial palace, startling the Jade Emperor himself.
The monkey learned to crawl, then to walk, and soon he bowed to the four quarters. He joined the other monkeys on the mountain, eating wild fruits, drinking from streams, and playing among the flowers. He knew neither sorrow nor fear, only the endless joy of existence.
One day, the monkeys gathered at a waterfall cascading down the cliff. "Whoever dares to leap through that waterfall and discovers what lies behind it," they declared, "shall be our king!"
The stone monkey did not hesitate. He closed his eyes, crouched low, and leapt through the curtain of water. When he opened his eyes, he found himself inside a vast stone cavern. An iron bridge spanned a flowing stream. A stone tablet at the entrance read: "The Blessed Land of the Flower-Fruit Mountain, The Cave Heaven of the Water Curtain."
The monkey returned and called the others in. Delighted beyond measure, the monkeys appointed the stone monkey as their king, addressing him as the Handsome Monkey King. For three hundred years, he ruled the mountain in carefree contentment.
But one day, joy faded. The Monkey King sat alone and wept. When his subjects asked why, he replied: "We may be happy now, but we are not beyond the reach of Yama, the King of Hell. One day, we shall all die."
A wise old monkey spoke: "My king, to escape the cycle of death, you must seek the way of the immortals, the Buddhas, and the sages. They alone dwell beyond the Wheel of Reincarnation."
The Handsome Monkey King's heart was filled with determination. He built a raft from pine logs, took a bamboo pole for an oar, and set out alone across the great ocean. No monkey had ever dared venture so far.
Winds and waves battered his tiny raft. Days passed, then weeks. He drifted through storms that would have drowned lesser beings, through seas where great sea serpents roamed. But the stone monkey pressed on, driven by a hunger stronger than any fear.
At last, he reached the Southern Continent, the land of men. He shed his leaves and grass, dressed himself in human clothes, and walked among the people. They stared at his strange appearance — the fur on his face, the mischievous glint in his eyes.
For eight years, he wandered the world of men, learning their languages, their customs, and their petty concerns. He saw greed and kindness, war and peace, love and betrayal. But nowhere did he find what he truly sought — a master who could teach him the way of immortality.
Finally, he heard rumors of a great sage who lived on the Mountain of the Heart and Mind. The sage had transcended the mortal realm and could teach the secrets of eternal life. The Monkey King gathered his remaining strength and climbed.
The mountain was treacherous — cliffs that scraped the sky, paths that wound like serpents, and a silence so profound it seemed to swallow all sound. Near the summit, he found a woodcutter singing a strange song about the unity of all things.
"Good sir," said the Monkey King, bowing, "your song speaks of profound truths. Might you be the immortal sage I seek?" The woodcutter laughed: "I am only a woodcutter. The immortal you seek dwells in the Cave of the Slanting Moon and Three Stars, further up the mountain."
At the cave's entrance, the Monkey King hesitated. Through the stone doors, he could hear the faint chanting of sutras. He knelt and waited, not daring to knock, not daring to leave. Three days and three nights he knelt.
A young acolyte opened the door. "My master bids you enter." The Monkey King scrambled inside, where a venerable sage sat upon a raised platform, his white beard flowing like a waterfall of silk. This was Patriarch Subodhi.
"Where do you come from?" asked the Patriarch. "I come from the Eastern Continent, from the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit," the monkey answered. "Liar!" the Patriarch thundered. "The Eastern Continent is separated by two great oceans. No mortal could cross them. Throw him out!"
The Monkey King prostrated himself. "Master, I am no liar. I crossed the oceans on a raft of pine, guided by nothing but the stars and my determination. I wandered for eight years through the world of men, seeking you and only you."
The Patriarch's stern face softened. "Since you have come so far and endured so much, I will teach you. Henceforth you shall be called Sun Wukong — the Monkey Awakened to Emptiness." And so the Handsome Monkey King became Sun Wukong, and his true journey began.
